hops.title: Compare it: soccer cleats and earthworm bristles
hops.text: Soccer cleats and bumpy sneakers have little studs that keep your child from sliding on grass. A common nightcrawler has many rings along its body, and most rings carry eight tiny bristles called setae that dig in the same way. Those bristles make the faint scratchy sound on the paper towel.

hops.afterHeading: Questions to ask while you do it
hops.title: Ask it: what underground room would you pick?
hops.text: Before you lift the cardboard, ask your child, "If you lived underground with no arms, no legs and no flashlight, what would your favorite room feel like?" Kids might answer cozy, dark, squishy or quiet. Every answer is welcome. Then follow up warmly: "Let's peek and count how many worms are on each side."

sources.citation: University of Illinois Extension, "My Body," The Adventures of Herman the Worm

hops.title: Point at it: worm tunnels in the lawn
hops.text: After rain, walk a shady lawn or park edge with your child and look closely, without poking or touching. Spot small round holes with bits of leaf or plant debris pulled into the top. Some of these are nightcrawler tunnels, which can drop five or six feet straight down, nearly as tall as you.

audio.title: Three easy ways to talk about earthworms with your child
audio.transcript:
Here are three easy ideas to bring along when you do the earthworm tray test with your child.

First, the cleats. When you hear that soft scratching on the paper towel, grab one of your child's bumpy sneakers or soccer cleats and flip it over. Those little studs keep feet from sliding on grass. A common nightcrawler has many rings along its body, and most of its rings carry eight tiny bristles called setae. They grip the paper the same way, so the worm does not slip backward as it crawls.

Second, a question. Before you lift the cardboard, ask your child what their favorite room would feel like if they lived underground with no arms, no legs and no flashlight. You might hear cozy, or dark, or squishy, or quiet. Every answer is welcome. Then say, let's peek and count how many worms are on each side.

Third, a walk. After the next rain, stroll along a shady lawn edge and look closely, without poking or touching. Watch for small round holes with bits of leaf or plant debris pulled into the top. Some of those are nightcrawler tunnels, and they can drop five or six feet straight down, nearly as tall as a grown-up. Here is a fun number to share: in healthy soil, earthworms can make more than eight hundred thousand small channels in a single acre, and those channels carry rainwater down into the ground.

So the next time you spot a worm, you have a whole hidden neighborhood under your feet to wonder about together.
